Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex. Its **geometric realization**
$|K|$ is the set of functions $\alpha:V \to [0,1]$ such that:

1. $\alpha(v)=0$ for all but finitely many $v \in V$;
2. $\sum_{v \in V}\alpha(v)=1$;
3. the support $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha):=\{v \in V:\alpha(v)\neq 0\}$ is a simplex of $K$.

For each simplex $\sigma=\{v_0,\dots,v_n\}$ of $K$, write
$$|\sigma|:=\{\alpha \in |K| : \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq \sigma\}.$$
Sending $\alpha$ to the barycentric tuple
$(\alpha(v_0),\dots,\alpha(v_n))$ identifies $|\sigma|$ with the geometric
simplex spanned by the standard basis vectors indexed by $v_0,\dots,v_n$, so
$|\sigma|$ carries its Euclidean simplex topology.

We give $|K|$ the **weak topology** with respect to these simplex inclusions:
a subset $U\subseteq |K|$ is declared open exactly when $U\cap|\sigma|$ is open
in $|\sigma|$ for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$.

For finite $K$, the weak topology on $|K|$ equals the Euclidean subspace topology in $\mathbb R^{V(K)}$; $|K|$ is compact, metrizable and Hausdorff. If $P$ is a finite subcomplex of any $K$, then $|P|\hookrightarrow|K|$ is a closed embedding, with that same finite Euclidean topology.

If $K$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, then its geometric realization
$|K|$ is compact and Hausdorff.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Two constructions are defined here, one for maps *into* spaces and one for maps
*out of* spaces. Every further construction on this page is an instance of one of
them.

**Initial topology.** Let $X$ be a set, let $I$ be an index set, let
$(Y_i, \mathcal{T}_i)$ be a topological space for each $i \in I$
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $f_i : X \to Y_i$ be a function for each
$i$. The **initial topology** on $X$ induced by the family $(f_i)_{i \in I}$ is

$$\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{in}} \;:=\; \big\langle\, \{\, f_i^{-1}[V] : i \in I,\ V \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\} \,\big\rangle ,$$

the topology generated by the preimages of the open sets of the $Y_i$
([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

*This is well posed, and the obligation is discharged by the item cited.* For an
arbitrary family $\mathcal{S}$ of subsets of $X$, the family
$\langle \mathcal{S} \rangle$ is a topology on $X$, contains $\mathcal{S}$, and
is contained in every topology on $X$ containing $\mathcal{S}$
([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]); no further verification is needed here. By
[[thm-basis-criterion]] a **basis** for $\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{in}}$ is the family
of intersections of finitely many sets $f_i^{-1}[V]$, the intersection of none
being $X$.

**Final topology.** Let $X$ be a set, let $(Z_i, \mathcal{S}_i)$ be a topological
space for each $i \in I$, and let $g_i : Z_i \to X$ be a function for each $i$.
The **final topology** on $X$ induced by the family $(g_i)_{i \in I}$ is

$$\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{fin}} \;:=\; \{\, U \subseteq X : g_i^{-1}[U] \in \mathcal{S}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\} .$$

*This is a topology, and the verification is carried out here rather than
assumed.* Preimage commutes with the three set operations named in the axioms:
$g_i^{-1}[\varnothing] = \varnothing$ and $g_i^{-1}[X] = Z_i$, which gives (T1);
$g_i^{-1}[\bigcup \mathcal{U}] = \bigcup \{\, g_i^{-1}[U] : U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$
for every family $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{fin}}$, which with
(T2) in $Z_i$ gives (T2); and
$g_i^{-1}[U \cap V] = g_i^{-1}[U] \cap g_i^{-1}[V]$, which with (T3) in $Z_i$
gives (T3) ([[def-topological-space]]).

**Two degenerate cases, stated because they are used.** For $I = \varnothing$ the
initial topology is $\langle \varnothing \rangle = \{\varnothing, X\}$, the
indiscrete topology, and the final topology is $\mathcal{P}(X)$, the discrete
topology, the defining condition being vacuous
([[def-standard-topologies]], [[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]). For a family
consisting of a single map the definitions read the same way with the index
dropped.

**The subspace topology is the model initial topology.** Let $(X,\mathcal{T})$ be
a space, let $S \subseteq X$ and let $\iota : S \to X$ be the inclusion. Then
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$, so the generating family for
the initial topology of the one-element family $(\iota)$ is exactly
$\mathcal{T}_S = \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\}$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). That family is already a topology, so generating
adds nothing and the initial topology of $\iota$ **is** the subspace topology.
Everything [[def-subspace-topology-top]] proves about it is therefore quoted here
and not reproved: its closed sets are the traces of the closed sets, a basis of
$X$ traces to a basis of $S$, the inclusion is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]),
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the coarsest topology making $\iota$ continuous, and a map
$g : Z \to S$ is continuous if and only if $\iota \circ g$ is.

**Terminology.** A family $(f_i)$ as above is the *defining family* of the
initial topology, and likewise for the final one; both topologies depend on the
whole family and not on any one member. The characteristic properties that make
these two constructions worth naming are the subject of the next item.

Let $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be topological spaces, with subspaces carrying the subspace
topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then:

1. **Composites.** If $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$ are continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) then $g \circ f : X \to Z$ is continuous.
2. **Open cover.** Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let
   $\{\, U_i : i \in I \,\}$ be a family of open subsets of $X$ with
   $\bigcup_{i \in I} U_i = X$. If $f|_{U_i} : U_i \to Y$ is continuous for every
   $i \in I$, then $f$ is continuous.
3. **Finite closed cover.** Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function, let $n \ge 1$ and
   let $F_1, \dots, F_n$ be closed subsets of $X$ with
   $F_1 \cup \dots \cup F_n = X$. If $f|_{F_k} : F_k \to Y$ is continuous for
   every $k$, then $f$ is continuous.

The converses of claims 2 and 3 hold with no hypothesis on the cover at all:
every restriction of a continuous map to a subspace is continuous
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). The finiteness in claim 3 is not removable; see
the remarks.

Let $f,g:X\to\mathbb R$ be continuous maps from a topological space. Then
$f+g$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, and $\min(f,g)$ are continuous. On the open
cozero set $\operatorname{coz}(g)$, the quotient $f/g$ is continuous. The same
holds for every finite sum, product, maximum, or minimum of continuous
real-valued maps.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

derivations.claim: Write $x_v$ for the barycentric coordinates of a point of $|K|$ and put $f_i(x)=\sum_{f(v)=i}x_v$, so that $f(x)=(f_i(x))_i$ is a convex combination. In every simplex of $K$ cut by the finitely many hyperplanes $f_i=f_j$ and take the resulting closed convex cells and all their faces; the same arrangement intersected with a simplex gives intersections as faces, so these cells form a finite polytopal subdivision of $K$. For a cell $C$ let $I(C)$ be the set of vertices $i$ such that $f_i$ is maximal on $C$; it is nonempty, and $I(C)\subseteq I(C')$ whenever $C'$ is a face of $C$. For every $i\in I(C)$ the image of $C$ under $f$ lies in the star of $i$, and the set $I(C)$ spans a simplex of $L$ contained in the image simplex. For every nonempty simplex $A$ on vertices in $I(C)$ include the join cell $A*C$ in the Euclidean join of $|L|$ and $|K|$, and include $|L|$ itself and every face of every such join. The join identities $(A*C)\cap(A'*C')=(A\cap A')*(C\cap C')$ and the face structure of the underlying cells make this a finite polytopal complex $T_f$ whose upper boundary is $|K|$ and whose lower boundary is $|L|$. A point of its relative interior has unique join coordinates $(1-t)y+tx$ with $0<t<1$, $y\in|L|$, $x\in|K|$, and lies in $T_f$ exactly when the support of $y$ consists of vertices where $f_i(x)$ attains its maximum.

Any finite polytopal complex $P$ is triangulated by induction on dimension: for each cell choose a point in its relative interior, having already chosen one for every proper face, and cone the already triangulated boundary from that point. Each ray from the interior point meets the boundary in exactly one point, the cones over cells have disjoint relative interiors and meet along the cones over their intersections, and the constructions agree on common faces, so this is a finite simplicial complex with the same underlying subset and the same dimension. Applied to the finite list of cells of $T_f$ (and to any finite sublist, coning subcomplexes first) it also respects unions of cells. Its dimension is at most $\max(\dim K+1,\dim L)$: if $C$ lies in a source simplex $\sigma$ with image simplex $\tau$, then $f|_\sigma$ is the affine surjection onto $\tau$, and the $k-1$ equations $f_i=f_j$ with $i,j\in I(C)$ (where $k=|I(C)|$) are independent on $\tau$; hence $\dim C\le\dim\sigma-(k-1)$ and $\dim(A*C)=k+\dim C\le\dim\sigma+1$ for every join cell, while the remaining lower cells have dimension at most $\dim L$. For each pair $(K_j,L_j)$ the cells with $C\subseteq|K_j|$ and $A\subseteq|L_j|$, together with $|L_j|$, form a subcomplex: faces of such cells again satisfy those inclusions, because $K_j$ and $L_j$ are subcomplexes and $f(K_j)\subseteq L_j$. The top preimage $f^{-1}(|L_j|)$ is a union of source faces, since $f$ is simplicial, hence a union of cells of the subdivision. One further barycentric subdivision makes all these subcomplexes full: its vertices are cells, and a chain all of whose vertices lie in a selected subcomplex is a chain of cells of that subcomplex.

For $x\in C$ and $i\in I(C)$ put $P_i(x)_v=x_v/f_i(x)$ when $f(v)=i$ and $P_i(x)_v=0$ otherwise. Since $f(x)$ is a point of the simplex $\tau\subseteq L$, some coordinate $f_i(x)$ is at least $1/N$ with $N$ the number of vertices of $L$, so the denominators are bounded below on every cell and $P_i$ is continuous on $C$ with values in the face of the source simplex over $i$. Define $H$ on the join cell $A*C$ by $H((1-t)y+tx)=[u,t]$, where $u=t\,x+(1-t)\sum_{i\in A}y_iP_i(x)$ and the bracket denotes the class in $M_f$ of the point $(u,t)\in|K|\times[0,1]$. The vector $u$ is a convex combination of points of the source simplex, so it lies in $|K|$, and $f(u)=t\,f(x)+(1-t)y$. For $0<t<1$ the join coordinates of a point are unique, and on intersections $A*C\cap A'*C'$ the representation has $y\in A\cap A'$, $x\in C\cap C'$, so the values agree; at $t=1$ the value is $[x,1]$ and at $t=0$ it is $[u,0]=f(u)=y$, the lower point itself, so the formula is well defined and fixes both boundary copies. It is continuous on each closed cell, because the $P_i$ are continuous and the map $(u,t)\mapsto[u,t]$ is the composite of a continuous map with the quotient projection; by the finite closed-cover form of [F2] it is continuous on all of $T_f$.

Define a map $\Psi$ on $|K|\times[0,1]\sqcup|L|$ as follows: $\Psi$ is the identity on $|L|$; for $u\in|K|$ and $0\le t<1$ put $z=f(u)$ and let $m=m(u,t)>0$ be the unique number with $\sum_i\min(z_i,m)=t$ (unique because the left side is continuous, vanishes at $m=0$, is strictly increasing while below $\sum_iz_i=1$, and $t<1$), and set $v_i=\min(z_i,m)/t$ for $t>0$, $y_i=(z_i-m)_+/(1-t)$, and $x_w=(v_{f(w)}/z_{f(w)})u_w$ when $z_{f(w)}>0$ and $x_w=0$ otherwise; at $t=1$ set $x=u$ and $y$ arbitrary in the join point $u$. Then $z=t\,v+(1-t)y$ with $v,y$ probability vectors, $f(x)=v$, and $x$ lies in every source simplex containing $u$; moreover $x_w=u_w/t$ when $z_{f(w)}\le m$ and $x_w=m\,u_w/(t\,z_{f(w)})$ when $z_{f(w)}\ge m$, so the formulas are continuous on their finitely many closed regions with denominators bounded below by $t/N$ on each collar $t\ge t_0>0$ and extend continuously to $t=0$ with value $y=f(u)$ and to $t=1$ with value $x=u$. Hence $\Psi$ is continuous and satisfies $\Psi(u,0)=f(u)=\Psi(f(u))$, so it respects the equivalence relation and descends to a continuous map $\Phi:M_f\to T_f$. The two constructions are inverse: substituting $H$'s formula into the threshold equations recovers $\sum_i\min(z_i,m)=t$ and returns the given $[u,t]$, while for a join point $(1-t)y+tx\in T_f$ and $u=t\,x+(1-t)\sum y_iP_i(x)$ one computes $z_i=t f_i(x)+(1-t)y_i\le t\max_jf_j(x)=:m$ when $y_i=0$, and $z_i=m+(1-t)y_i$ with $f_i(x)=\max_jf_j(x)$ when $y_i>0$; the threshold equation then determines $m=t\max_jf_j(x)$, and the normalized coordinates of $u$ recover $x$ and $y$ as $(t+(1-t)y_i/f_i(x))x_w=u_w$. So $H\circ\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Phi\circ H=\mathrm{id}$, and the continuous bijection $H$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $\Phi$.

The retraction $R$ of the cylinder onto $|L|$, read through $H$, is $R((1-t)y+tx)=(1-t)y+t\,f(x)$ on each join cell, an affine map that is piecewise linear after step 2.1. For a pair $(K_j,L_j)$ the formula of step 3.1 preserves the subcylinder over $f^{-1}(|L_j|)\times[0,1]\cup|L_j|$, and the inverse formulas of step 4.1 have source support contained in the support of $u$, so the preimage of that subcylinder is exactly the subcomplex described in step 2.1, including the retained $f^{-1}(|L_j|)$ on the top boundary. Finally, on each join cell with $t$ bounded away from zero the map $H$ is given by rational functions of the affine coordinates with denominators bounded away from zero, hence is smooth there in the ambient affine coordinates; nothing is asserted about differentiability at the collapsed end $t=0$, where the quotient is not a manifold chart. This proves all asserted clauses.

boundaries.evidence: The collection of pairs $(K_j,L_j)$ in the Statement may be empty, and step 5.1 attaches the corresponding subpolyhedra one at a time, so the empty list imposes no cell and no subdivision.

boundaries.reason: Step 3.1 divides only by the weights $f_i(x)$, which are bounded below by $1/N$ on each cell before the division, so no zero denominator is reached.

boundaries.evidence: A one-vertex source is the case $dim K=0$ of step 1.1: the hyperplane arrangement is trivial and the join formulas of step 4.1 triangulate the resulting cone on a point.

Vertex identifications are explicitly allowed, so collapsings are not excluded; steps 3.1 and 4.1 index cells by the fibres of $f$ and define the threshold $m$ whenever the collapsed weights are positive.
The two ends are $t=0$, where the identification $xsim f(x)$ is imposed, and $t=1$; step 4.1 defines the map separately there and verifies both inverse identities at these ends.

The lemma asserts the existence of a triangulation with listed properties rather than a characterization, so no implication direction is owed.
No converse is claimed: the lemma does not assert that only mapping cylinders admit such finite triangulations.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Let $W$ be a compact finite smooth Whitney-stratified subset of a
smooth Euclidean ambient space, with the frontier condition. After shrinking
compatible tube data and smoothly rescaling their squared radii by positive
functions of their base projections, there are normalized tubes
$T_X=\{\rho_X<1\}$ and stratum-preserving radial projections
$R_X(s):T_X\setminus X\to\{\rho_X=s\}$ for $0<s<1$. On every incident overlap
$Y<X$ they satisfy
$$R_X(s)R_Y(t)=R_Y(t)R_X(s),\qquad \rho_YR_X(s)=\rho_Y,\qquad \rho_XR_Y(t)=\rho_X,$$
whenever the source and target points lie in the indicated retained tubes. They
also satisfy $\pi_XR_X(s)=\pi_X$, $R_X(s)R_X(t)=R_X(s)$, and
$\pi_ZR_X(s)=R_X(s)|_Z\pi_Z$ for $X<Z$ on overlaps. They are continuous on their
stratified domains and smooth on individual strata. For a fixed reference
$a\in(0,1)$, $(R_X(a),\rho_X)$ identifies the punctured tube with
$S_X(a)\times(0,1)$, where $S_X(a)=W\cap\{\rho_X=a\}$; adjoining $X$ identifies
it with the corresponding open mapping cylinder of $\pi_X:S_X(a)\to X$. This is
a controlled topological collar; no semialgebraicity of the resulting flows is
asserted.

Let $f:K\to L$ be a simplicial map of finite complexes; vertex identifications
are allowed. Its topological mapping cylinder
$$M_f=(|K|\times[0,1]\sqcup|L|)/((x,0)\sim f(x))$$
has a finite triangulation of dimension at most $\max(\dim K+1,\dim L)$ and a
homeomorphism $H$ to $M_f$ fixing both boundary copies. The triangulated
cylinder retraction to $|L|$ is piecewise linear. Before triangulating, its
cells and $H$ have the explicit formulas in the proof. For every finite
collection of pairs of subcomplexes $(K_j,L_j)$ with $f(K_j)\subseteq L_j$, the
corresponding cylinders are subpolyhedra; one simultaneous subdivision makes
them subcomplexes. The construction also retains the top subpolyhedron
$f^{-1}(|L_j|)$ for each $L_j$. On each cell away from the collapsed end, $H$
is smooth in affine coordinates; no immersion or smooth tangent-star claim is
made at a collapsed end. All boundaries may be subdivided: the lemma does not
promise an extension of an arbitrarily fixed boundary triangulation without
subdivision.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Every local corner face, and any specified finite union of such closed faces, is
a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\pi:E\to B$ be a smooth bundle with compact
total space, compact smooth base and compact smooth fibre, permitting corners.
A bundle here comes with finite smooth local product trivializations, whose
transition maps preserve all local source/target corner faces; a boundary face
in a product chart is either a base face or a fibre face. Let $h:D\to B$ be a
supplied finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.

Then there is a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation $F:K\to E$
and a piecewise affine map $r:K\to D$ with $\pi F=hr$. Thus the actual bundle
projection is PL over the fixed base parametrization. Refining base pieces for
local construction does not change $h$ or the original complex $D$ in the final
diagram: $r$ on a domain simplex is affine into a simplex of the original $D$.

The construction is relative to any supplied finite diagram $C:J\to E$,
$\pi C=hr_J$, embedding onto a closed neighbourhood of a protected subpolyhedron
$R$ contained in its relative interior, provided the fitting supports of the
remaining pieces can be chosen disjoint from $R$. In particular this applies
when $C$ is an already triangulated collar neighbourhood of the entire boundary
and $R$ is a smaller collar: the original boundary and all its corner-face
intersections are kept pointwise, with compatible subdivisions allowed. All
union intersections are full subcomplexes.

This relative contract requires the **collar diagram**, not just an arbitrary
triangulation of the boundary without any projection-preserving neighbourhood
extension. Nor does proper smoothness of $\pi$ alone replace the supplied bundle
trivializations.

Let $F:K\to M$ and $G:L\to M$ be whole-star smooth embeddings of finite complexes
into a smooth manifold without boundary. Given any positive strong $C^1$
tolerance, there are approximations on finite subdivisions fitting in a full
subcomplex whose union is a whole-star smooth embedding.

The same conclusion holds for bundle diagrams $\pi F=hr_K$, $\pi G=hr_L$ over a
fixed whole-star smooth base embedding $h:D\to B$, when all relevant images are
in a smooth bundle with product trivializations. The final approximations
satisfy these **same** diagrams with $h$ and $r_K,r_L$ unchanged as point maps,
so the bundle projection is preserved exactly. The union map has the induced
affine map to $D$.

The construction may be supported in a prescribed open neighbourhood $V$ of the
new piece being fitted, including only the old pieces whose images meet that
neighbourhood. In particular it fixes a closed protected region $R$ pointwise
whenever all newly processed pieces and their required closed stars have images
in $V$, with $\overline V\cap R=\varnothing$, and the maps already fit on the
pieces outside this support. This is the fixed-collar relative interface: it
does not assert arbitrary pointwise fixed-side fitting without the
neighbourhood/separation hypotheses. Additional local affine plane constraints
are preserved if the chosen charts make them coordinate planes and the already
supplied diagrams respect them. For corner targets the same construction applies
when all pieces satisfy the adapted face/tangent hypotheses of
[[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]] in these
charts; that lemma proves every altered piece remains in its original orthant.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $p\in M$, and suppose $F$ has constant rank
$r$ on a neighbourhood of $p$. Then there are smooth charts
$\varphi:U\to\mathbb R^m$ at $p$ and $\psi:V\to\mathbb R^n$ at $F(p)$ such that

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}(u,v)=(u,0)$$

for $(u,v)\in\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^{m-r}$ near $\varphi(p)$, with the zero
in $\mathbb R^{n-r}$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $W$ be compact with finite compatible tube data and the actual commuting radial collars of [F1]. Retain outer maps while using inner normalized domains. Fix a stratum $X$ and a level $0<a<1$; write $A=\{p\in T_X:\rho_X(p)=a\}$ and $L=\overline A$ in $W$, which is compact. A limit of points of $A$ leaving $T_X$ must land on the frontier of $X$: in tube parameters either the bases have an interior limit, which retains the tube because the normalized radius is the fixed $a<1$, or the bases approach the frontier, where the imposed displacement bound forces the point and its base to have the same limit. Consequently $L$ meets only upper incident strata, where it is the smooth hypersurface $\rho_X=a$, and lower frontier strata of $X$; it misses $X$ itself and incomparable strata.

Membership in $L$ on a lower frontier stratum $Y<X$ is locally constant along $Y$, by transport rather than by an appeal to a Whitney property of $L$. On a small $Y$-base coordinate box construct smooth lifts of each base coordinate field in increasing dimension, with the maximal incident tube controller as in [F1]; the field on $Y$ is the given coordinate field and upper fields satisfy $d\pi_ZV=V_Z\pi_Z$ and $d\rho_ZV=0$ on the retained tube of every lower $Z$. On the $X$-tube the lift therefore preserves $\rho_X=a$. The compact-trapping proof of [F1] gives a jointly continuous short flow even without ambient boundedness on an entire outer tube, and it maps $A$ to itself wherever defined, hence maps its closure $L$ to itself, as does the inverse flow. Ordered coordinate transports along $Y$ prove local constancy of membership, so $L\cap Y$ is an open and closed union of components of $Y$.

The same horizontal-lift construction, with the level constraints imposed in the chain of controllers, shows that the closure-incidence label of an upper level piece is locally constant on each lower level piece. If a disconnected level piece has different incidence labels, split it by the finitely many Boolean labels recording membership in the closures of the finitely many upper pieces; these subsets are open and closed smooth pieces, and since there are at most finitely many labels this makes a finite frontier stratification without assuming finitely many connected components. The maps and collars below restrict to these pieces, because the transports preserve each closure and hence its incidence labels.

For a lower frontier $Y<X$ the restricted $Y$-tube retracts $L$ into $L\cap Y$: radial $Y$-transport preserves $\rho_X$ on $A$ by the commuting collar identities, and its limit as $\rho_Y\to0$ is $\pi_Y$, so $\pi_Y(A\cap T_Y)\subseteq L$ and continuity gives the same inclusion for $L\cap T_Y$. For an upper $Y>X$ the identity $\rho_X\pi_Y=\rho_X$ shows directly that $\pi_Y$ preserves the level hypersurface. Therefore all inherited projections have their actual target in the corresponding stratum of $L$.

The inherited radius/projection maps are submersive on the smooth strata of $L$. If $Y<X<Z$, then on $Z$ the map $(\pi_X,\rho_X)$ is submersive and $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y)$ factors through $\pi_X$, while the latter pair is submersive on $X$; hence the joint map $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y,\rho_X)$ is submersive on $Z$, and restricting to $\rho_X=a$ gives the full rank of $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y)$ there. If $X<Y<Z$, then $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y)$ is submersive on $Z$ and $\rho_X$ factors through $\pi_Y$; its restriction to the kernel of $d\rho_X$ surjects onto the tangent space of $(Y\cap\{\rho_X=a\})\times(0,1)$, because lifting a target vector with $d\rho_X=0$ through the original pair and using the factorization forces the lift to satisfy the same equation. This is precisely the needed level-pair submersion.

All control equations and incomparable-domain disjointness restrict, and local properness restricts because $L$ is closed in compact $W$. The radial families restrict too: they preserve $A$ where defined, preserve its closure by continuity, and preserve the new incidence labels; their semigroup, commutation and projection equations are the original equations on actual retained domains, and zero-end convergence still follows from the compact tube estimate. Thus $L$ is a compact finite smooth controlled stratified space with commuting collars. Its maximal stratum dimension is at most $\dim(W)-1$, since upper level strata lose one dimension and lower frontier strata have dimension strictly less than $\dim X\le\dim W$; this is the dimension drop needed by the interior triangulation induction. Nothing here identifies $L$ with an algebraic or semialgebraic set.

For each stratum $Z$ define its core by removing the small open tubes of lower-dimensional strata; compactness is literal. A sequence in this core tending to the frontier of $Z$ would eventually lie in the open tube of its limiting lower stratum, contradicting the definition, so the core is a closed subset of $W$ contained in $Z$, hence compact; the same argument applies to a level link after lower-stratum tubes are removed.

At a core point the active lower controllers form a chain and the differentials of their radius functions are independent on the stratum. For a chain $Y_1<\cdots<Y_k<Z$, the submersion $(\pi_{Y_k},\rho_{Y_k})$ on $Z$ and the factorizations of the earlier radius functions through $\pi_{Y_k}$ let one lift first through the earlier joint radius map and then through the maximal pair, proving surjectivity of the joint radius map on $Z$. In constant-rank coordinates the inequalities $\rho_{Y_j}\ge d_j$ are independent half-space coordinates, so the core is a smooth compact manifold with corners and every designated face or face intersection is a genuine corner face, which checks the corner-face compatibility premise of [F3] and [F4].

The normal level-core map to a fixed base core, $\pi_X:Z\cap S_X(a)\to X$, is a proper corner submersion with compatible faces. Gluing the finite core and collar complexes gives the interior triangulation, the already lower-dimensional pieces and their boundary projections retain their maps, and only finitely many $(n,p)$ assertions occur, so finitely many decreases of $d$ leave a positive final parameter.

Cone the face subdivisions using these points and barycentrically cone the target cells; nested source faces have nested image target faces, with repetitions allowed, so the resulting map is simplicial. Mark all intersections with future lower levels and stratum closures, and apply one further barycentric subdivision to make all these marked subcomplexes full.

Stratum-closure intersections are retained by the same subcylinder compatibility, because the radial maps preserve strata, so an upper stratum or its closure contributes its marked top subset together with the appropriate zero-end base subset. After all $i$ have been processed the image is $W$, and all strata and prescribed unions of strata are unions of open simplices. The finite list of glued complexes therefore supplies the claimed finite compatible stratified triangulation by the preceding interior construction and the exact relative-supplier premises.

Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex. Its **geometric realization**
$|K|$ is the set of functions $\alpha:V \to [0,1]$ such that:

1. $\alpha(v)=0$ for all but finitely many $v \in V$;
2. $\sum_{v \in V}\alpha(v)=1$;
3. the support $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha):=\{v \in V:\alpha(v)\neq 0\}$ is a simplex of $K$.

For each simplex $\sigma=\{v_0,\dots,v_n\}$ of $K$, write
$$|\sigma|:=\{\alpha \in |K| : \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq \sigma\}.$$
Sending $\alpha$ to the barycentric tuple
$(\alpha(v_0),\dots,\alpha(v_n))$ identifies $|\sigma|$ with the geometric
simplex spanned by the standard basis vectors indexed by $v_0,\dots,v_n$, so
$|\sigma|$ carries its Euclidean simplex topology.

We give $|K|$ the **weak topology** with respect to these simplex inclusions:
a subset $U\subseteq |K|$ is declared open exactly when $U\cap|\sigma|$ is open
in $|\sigma|$ for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$.

Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex.

A **subcomplex** of $K$ is a subfamily $L \subseteq K$ that is itself closed
under taking subsets.

If $\sigma \in K$, its **closure** is the subcomplex
$$\overline{\sigma}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma\}.$$
More generally, if $A \subseteq K$, its closure is
$$\overline{A}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma \text{ for some } \sigma \in A\}.$$

For a simplex $\sigma \in K$, the **closed star** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{St}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \sigma \cup \tau \in K\},$$
and the **open star** is the union, after realization, of the relative
interiors of simplices $\rho\in K$ with $\sigma\subseteq\rho$.

The **link** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{Lk}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \tau \cap \sigma=\varnothing \text{ and } \sigma \cup \tau \in K\}.$$

For finite $K$, the weak topology on $|K|$ equals the Euclidean subspace topology in $\mathbb R^{V(K)}$; $|K|$ is compact, metrizable and Hausdorff. If $P$ is a finite subcomplex of any $K$, then $|P|\hookrightarrow|K|$ is a closed embedding, with that same finite Euclidean topology.

If $K$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, then its geometric realization
$|K|$ is compact and Hausdorff.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

derivations.claim: Put $L=|\operatorname{lk}_K\sigma|$ and let $E=\{rq:0\le r<1,\ q\in L\}$ inside the Euclidean coordinate space on the vertices of the link, with the subspace topology. For an empty link both the cone by convention and $E=\{0\}$ are a single apex, so assume $L\ne\varnothing$. The continuous map $L\times[0,1)\to E$, $(q,r)\mapsto rq$, identifies exactly $L\times\{0\}$ with the apex: if $rq=r'q'$ with $r,r'>0$, coordinate sums give $r=r'$ and then $q=q'$. It therefore descends to a continuous bijection $\varphi:c_{<1}(L)\to E$. For each $0<t<1$, the closed radial cone $(L\times[0,t])/(L\times\{0\})$ is compact by [F2], and its continuous bijection onto $E_t=\{rq:0\le r\le t,\ q\in L\}$ is a homeomorphism because $E_t$ is Hausdorff. Away from the apex the inverse on the full open cone is continuous by $r=\sum_vz_v$, $q=z/r$, followed by the quotient projection. At the apex, the preimage of any quotient-open neighbourhood is an open set containing $L\times\{0\}$. Product neighbourhoods of its points, a finite cover of the compact link $L$, and the minimum of their positive radii give an $\epsilon>0$ with $L\times[0,\epsilon)$ in that preimage. The relatively open set $\{z\in E:\sum_vz_v<\epsilon\}$ is consequently mapped by $\varphi^{-1}$ into the given neighbourhood. Thus the inverse is continuous at the apex too, and $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism of the full open cone.

For a point $x$ of the open star put $a=\sum_{v\in\sigma}x_v>0$, set $p_v=x_v/a$ for $v\in\sigma$ and $z_v=x_v$ for $v\notin\sigma$. Then $p\in\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|$, $r:=\sum_vz_v=1-a<1$, and the support of $x$ is $\sigma\cup\operatorname{supp}(z)$, so $\operatorname{supp}(z)$, if nonempty, is a simplex of the link. Conversely, given $p\in\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|$ and $z\in E$ with $r=\sum_vz_v$, define a coordinate family by $x_v=(1-r)p_v$ on $\sigma$ and $x_v=z_v$ off $\sigma$; it is nonnegative with sum one, and its support is $\sigma\cup\operatorname{supp}(z)$, a simplex of $K$ because $\operatorname{supp}(z)$ is a simplex of the link. The two constructions are mutually inverse: from $x$ one recovers $a=1-r$ and $z$, hence $x$; from $(p,z)$ one recovers $p$ from the normalized $\sigma$-coordinates and $z$ from the outside coordinates. Both are continuous, the only division being by $a>0$ on the open star for the forward map, while the inverse is a polynomial expression in $(p,z)$ and the continuous function $r=\sum_vz_v$. By step 1.1 the second factor is the cone $c_{<1}(L)$, and since $\operatorname{supp}(z)$ records exactly which link simplex the radial coordinate lies over, each simplex interior containing $\sigma$ is carried to the product of the corresponding link-simplex interior with $(0,1)$, while points with $z=0$ map to $\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|\times\{$apex$\}$ and the simplex $\sigma$ itself to the apex. Thus the star is homeomorphic to the stated product.

The open star is open in $|K|$ because it is the finite intersection, over the vertices of $\sigma$, of the sets on which one barycentric coordinate is positive, each open in the weak topology by definition. The link is a subcomplex of the finite complex $K$, hence it has finitely many simplices and compact realization by [F2]. Finally, if a point $x$ of the star lay in $|D|$, its support would be a simplex $\rho$ of $D$ with $\sigma\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(x)=\rho$; the subcomplex $D$ is closed under taking faces, so $\sigma\in D$, contradicting $\sigma\notin D$. Hence the star is disjoint from $|D|$.

boundaries.evidence: When the link is empty the Statement declares the cone to be a single apex, and step 1.1 realizes this directly as the one-point space ${0}$ with the subspace topology.
The radial coordinate $r=1-a$ vanishes exactly at the apex; step 2.1 defines the inverse there and the quotient presentation of $c_{<1}$ is what makes the zero-radius point well defined.
If $sigma$ is a single vertex whose link is empty, step 1.1 identifies the cone factor with the apex and the chart is the identity on the interior of $|sigma|$.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate simplex is admitted: $sigma$ is required nonempty and the link uses only simplices disjoint from it, so no face-containment parameter degenerates.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 proves inverse continuity at radius zero by a uniform positive radius obtained from compactness of the link; compactness is used only on each closed radial subcone with radius t<1. Step 2.1 gives the inverse formula on the full half-open radial range.

boundaries.reason: No choice principle is used; the barycentric splitting of step 2.1 is an explicit formula and the simplex incidences are read off from the finite complex $K$.
The Statement displays a homeomorphism and lists its properties; it states no biconditional, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse classification is claimed; the lemma does not characterize which open subsets of $|K|$ arise as open stars.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on an arbitrary space $X$. For a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$, write $v_i=\sigma(e_i)$ and $\gamma_{01}^\sigma(t)=\sigma(1-t,t,0,\ldots,0)$.

The **intrinsic singular local chain group** is
$$C_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\bigoplus_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0}.$$
Write an element of the $\sigma$-summand as $m\sigma$. Its boundary is
$$\partial(m\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}(m)(\sigma\delta_0)+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^im(\sigma\delta_i),$$
and the boundary of a zero-simplex is zero. The exceptional zeroth face transports its coefficient from the old first vertex $v_0$ to the new first vertex $v_1$; all other faces keep $v_0$.

The **intrinsic singular local cochain group** is the product
$$C^n_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\prod_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0},$$
so a cochain $\varphi$ assigns $\varphi(\sigma)\in\mathcal L_{v_0}$ to every simplex, with no finite-support requirement. Its positive coboundary, consistent with [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]], is
$$(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(\sigma\delta_0)\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\delta_i).$$
Now the exceptional face value is transported back from $v_1$ to $v_0$.

For $A\subseteq X$, restrict $\mathcal L$ along the inclusion and set
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)/C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L),\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=\ker\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)\to C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L)\bigr).$$

For a connected CW complex with chosen basepoint $x$, universal cover $\widetilde X$, $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and base fiber $M=\mathcal L_x$ carrying $g m=T_{\bar g}m$, the equivalent universal-cover models are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
The first tensor product is the balanced construction of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] using the right action of [[def-right-group-ring-action-on-the-chains-of-a-universal-cover]]. For the second, convert that right chain module to a left one by
$$g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}.$$
Thus an equivariant cochain has the correctly typed rule
$$\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c),$$
not a module-Hom between one right and one left module.

The intrinsic/tensor identification sends $\widetilde\sigma\otimes m$ to the simplex $\sigma=p\widetilde\sigma$ with coefficient obtained by transporting $m$ along the path represented by $\widetilde\sigma(e_0)$. If $\widetilde\sigma$ is replaced by $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g$, that path is changed by the loop $g^{-1}$ and the coefficient becomes the transport of $gm$, exactly the balanced relation. The analogous statement for cochains proves the displayed equivariance rule. These maps respect the two boundary formulas term by term.

The **cellular local chain and cochain groups** of a connected CW complex are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
For a CW pair, quotient by the lifted subcomplex before tensoring and use the corresponding relative cellular complex before applying equivariant Hom. For a disconnected CW complex, take the direct sum of chain complexes and the degreewise product of cochain complexes over its components. Universal-cover coordinates of this componentwise description require a supplied basepoint in each component; the intrinsic complexes require no simultaneous basepoint choice and remain the definition when no such family is supplied.

The next lemma proves square-zero and independence of supplied lift bases. Empty spaces and negative degrees give zero groups, the zero local system gives the zero complexes, and constant systems reduce to the ordinary formulas because every transport is the identity.

Let $X$ be a nonempty connected finite CW complex with supplied characteristic maps, let $x\in X$ be a basepoint, put $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and let
$$p:\widetilde X\longrightarrow X$$
be a chosen universal cover, which exists for the spaces considered here because a finite CW complex is locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected ([[thm-universal-cover-existence]]). Write $R=\mathbb Z[\pi]$ for the integral group ring, a unital ring with basis the classes $[g]$ of the group elements ([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

**Lifted CW structure.** Every open cell $e\subseteq X$ is contractible, so $p^{-1}(e)$ splits into components each mapped homeomorphically onto $e$; such a component is an **open cell of $\widetilde X$ over $e$**. To obtain its **lifted characteristic map**, choose a point above the image of one interior point of the characteristic disk and lift the entire characteristic map $D^n\to X$ through $p$; this is possible because $D^n$ is simply connected ([[thm-covering-space-lifting-criterion]]), and its interior maps homeomorphically onto the chosen component over $e$. The inverse $e\to p^{-1}(e)$ alone cannot be composed with the characteristic map on its boundary, where that inverse is undefined. These lifted characteristic maps give the standard lifted CW structure ([[def-cell-attachment-by-a-characteristic-map]], [[def-skeleta-cw-subcomplex-and-relative-cw-complex]]). Its $n$-skeleton is
$$\widetilde X^n:=p^{-1}(X^n),$$
the union of the closed lifted cells over the cells of $X$ of dimension at most $n$; for a CW pair $(X,A)$ the preimage $p^{-1}(A)$ is a CW subcomplex of $\widetilde X$ and $p^{-1}(X^n\cup A)=p^{-1}(X^n)\cup p^{-1}(A)$ is the $n$-skeleton of the relative lifted structure.

**Deck action.** Identify $\pi$ with the deck group of $p$ by the no-reversal isomorphism of [[thm-deck-group-of-a-universal-cover-is-the-fundamental-group]], writing $T_g$ for the covering homeomorphism attached to $g\in\pi$; thus $T_1=\mathrm{id}$, $T_{gh}=T_g\circ T_h$, and every $T_g$ carries lifted cells onto lifted cells of the same dimension. A deck transformation is determined by its value at one point and acts freely, so the lifts of a single cell $e$ are exactly the cells $T_g\widetilde e$ for one chosen lift $\widetilde e$.

**Right group-ring action.** The action of the deck group on the singular and cellular chains of $\widetilde X$ is written on the left and the length-preserving insertion of inverses makes it a right action of $R$ by
$$c\cdot g:=T_g^{-1}(c)=T_{g^{-1}}(c),\qquad g\in\pi,$$
extended $\mathbb Z$-bilinearly in $c$ and the group-ring coefficient ([[def-relative-singular-homology]], [[def-oriented-cellular-chain-group]]); in particular $(c\cdot g)\cdot h=c\cdot gh$. Each $T_{g^{-1}}$ is a homeomorphism of pairs $(\widetilde X^n,\widetilde X^{n-1})\to(\widetilde X^n,\widetilde X^{n-1})$ and of pairs $(\widetilde X^n\cup p^{-1}A,\widetilde X^{n-1}\cup p^{-1}A)$, so the action passes to the homology of those pairs.

**Based cellular chains.** For each cell $e$ of $X$ choose an orientation of $e$, that is, an orientation of the disk of its characteristic map, and choose one oriented lift $\widetilde e$ carrying that orientation. Put
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R):=H_n(\widetilde X^n,\widetilde X^{n-1};\mathbb Z),$$
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X,p^{-1}(A);R):=H_n\bigl(\widetilde X^n\cup p^{-1}(A),\,\widetilde X^{n-1}\cup p^{-1}(A);\mathbb Z\bigr).$$
The notation after the semicolon records the **deck-induced $R$-module structure**; the homology coefficients are integral. By [[thm-relative-homology-of-consecutive-cw-skeleta]] these integral homology groups are free abelian on the lifted cells. The right action above makes them finite free right $R$-modules on one chosen oriented lift of each cell of $X$ (respectively each relative cell of $(X,A)$): the lifts of one cell form the $\pi$-orbit $\{T_g\widetilde e\}$, and $[g]\mapsto T_{g^{-1}}\widetilde e$ bijects $\pi$ with that orbit. Using $R$ as a second homology coefficient group here would duplicate the lift-indexed generators and would not yield the claimed rank. Degrees without relative cells give the zero module, and for a disconnected finite $X$ the construction is applied componentwise with its component group ring.

Assume AC. For a CW pair $(X,A)$ and local system $\mathcal L$, the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients:
$$H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
For a connected pair, it is the equivariant-Hom complex on cellular chains after the published right chain action is converted to the left action $g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}$; equivalently its cochains satisfy $\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c)$. The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice**, through
[[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]. Then every vector space $V$
over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) has a basis ([[def-linear-basis]]).

In particular the zero space has a basis, namely $\varnothing$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $F$ be a free $R$-module with basis indexed by $X$.

1. Assuming the Axiom of Choice, $F$ is projective and therefore flat.
2. If $X$ is finite, only finite choice is needed for projectivity; if $X=\varnothing$, no choice is needed.
3. Regardless of choice, $F$ is flat, because tensoring with $F$ is a direct sum of copies of the identity tensor functor.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M$ be an $R$-module. The module $M$ is **flat** if the functor $-\otimes_RM$ preserves exact sequences: whenever $A\to B\to C$ is exact, so is

$$A\otimes_RM\longrightarrow B\otimes_RM\longrightarrow C\otimes_RM.$$

Since tensoring is always right exact ([[thm-right-exactness-of-tensor-products]], [[def-exact-and-short-exact-sequences-of-modules]]), the definition asks for the remaining left-hand exactness. Its equivalent formulation as preservation of injections is proved separately rather than built into the definition.

The module $M$ is **faithfully flat** if a sequence of $R$-modules is exact exactly when its tensor with $M$ is exact.

For a unital ring homomorphism $f:R\to S$ ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) between commutative rings, $S$ is an $R$-module by $r\cdot s=f(r)s$. The map $f$ is **flat**, respectively **faithfully flat**, when this $R$-module is flat, respectively faithfully flat.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Work first on one component, with basepoint $x$, group $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$ and fibre $M=L_x$. By [F1] the degree-$q$ term of the cellular local cochain complex is $\operatorname{Hom}_{k[\pi]}(P_q,M)$ with $P_q$ free over $k[\pi]$ on the finitely many relative $q$-cells of the component, so choosing that finite basis identifies it with the finite product $M^{n_q}$; since $M$ is finite-dimensional, the term is finite-dimensional, and it is zero for $q<0$ and for $q>d$. By [F2] the cohomology $H^q(X,A;L)$ is the cohomology of this complex, so it is finite-dimensional as a kernel, image or quotient of finite-dimensional spaces and vanishes outside $[0,d]$. For a disconnected pair the cochain complex is the degreewise product of the complexes of the finitely many components, and the same conclusions hold componentwise; the empty pair has the zero complex.

Let $k'$ be a field extension and give $M\otimes_kk'$ the induced $k'[\pi]$-module structure; these fibres with the extended transport maps form the local system $L\otimes_kk'$. The termwise map $\operatorname{Hom}_{k[\pi]}(P_q,M)\otimes_kk'\to\operatorname{Hom}_{k'[\pi]}(P_q\otimes_kk',M\otimes_kk')$, defined on a basis of the free module $P_q$, is an isomorphism, because both sides identify with $(M\otimes_kk')^{n_q}$; it is natural in the second variable and therefore intertwines the differentials, which are obtained by dualizing the same $k[\pi]$-linear cellular boundary of [F2]. Hence $C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;L)\otimes_kk'$ is isomorphic, as a complex, to $C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;L\otimes_kk')$.

By [F3] the field $k'$, viewed as a $k$-vector space, is free and hence flat, so tensoring over $k$ with $k'$ preserves exact sequences. Applying this to the kernel-image sequences of the complex of step 1.1 gives a canonical isomorphism $H^q\bigl(C^*\otimes_kk'\bigr)\cong H^q(C^*)\otimes_kk'$, which by step 2.1 and [F2] is the stated map $H^q(X,A;L)\otimes_kk'\to H^q(X,A;L\otimes_kk')$, natural in the coefficients. The finiteness, the vanishing outside $[0,d]$, and the isomorphism all hold separately on each component and for the empty pair, where both complexes vanish.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement includes the empty pair and the zero local system; the componentwise computation of step 1.1 then has no components, and finiteness and the tensor comparison hold vacuously.
The vanishing range $q<0$ and $q>d$ includes the zero-dimensional case $d=0$, where the tensor comparison of step 3.1 is applied to the single nonzero term.
A one-point component is the case of step 1.1 with trivial $pi$, where the cellular complex is $M$ in degree zero and both finiteness and scalar extension are immediate.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate parameter occurs; the local system has finite-dimensional fibres and the CW pair is an arbitrary finite pair, with no nondegeneracy hypothesis beyond finiteness.
The cutoff outside $[0,d]$ is a degree range, not a limiting endpoint: no boundary value or one-sided limit of a family is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes AC, consumed through the basis and flatness suppliers [F3] at step 3.1; the two-sided ideal comparison itself is finite.

boundaries.reason: Finiteness, vanishing and the isomorphism are asserted separately; the lemma states no biconditional, so no forward direction is owed.
There is no converse claim, for instance no assertion that finite-dimensionality of the groups characterizes finite CW pairs.
